endorsements.quote: Institutions integrating AI (either “autonomous” or decision support systems) could consider monitoring human-AI concordance rates to assess for overreliance and complacency, as well as incorporating manual proficiency quotas, with performance on these no-AI cases providing a baseline benchmark for detecting drift for both the AI and the human user.
Clinicians remain as the “pilot-in-command” and accountable for overall judgement, while the digital copilot can contribute consistency and precision.

We propose going beyond this to consider scenario-based simulation training that recreate contexts where AI fails in order to monitor human dependence on AI systems, and to train clinicians when to trust, when to question, and when to override their “digital co-pilot”.
However, it is not enough to be able to operate an AI tool.
Similarly, as AI becomes more routine, minimum unaided practice without AI support should be considered for practicing clinicians.

unlisted_practices: Benchmark clinicians' diagnostic performance without AI on a regular basis to detect skill erosion and deskilling.
Restrict trainees' access to AI tools in clinical care until basic clinical competency has been developed.
Conduct longitudinal monitoring of trainees' cognitive and procedural competence to detect never-skilling or mis-skilling.

Define foundational AI literacy and minimum digital and technical competencies for clinicians using AI, and maintain them through medical school, postgraduate training, and continuing professional development.
Introduce unannounced surprise breaks from AI in routine-use settings to assess clinicians' readiness to operate safely without automation.
Hold structured debriefs in which clinicians reflect on AI-supported decisions to reinforce accountability and situational awareness.
Judge AI explainability by its contribution to clinicians' operational understanding rather than by the depth or technical fidelity of explanations.
Define explicit recovery mechanisms, such as stepwise reduction of automation or switching to manual mode, for when clinicians lose understanding of AI function or the AI fails.
Regulate the human-AI team and its competence, accountability, and situational awareness, beyond certifying AI as a medical device.
Invest in governance and infrastructure for human-AI collaboration in healthcare.
